learningObjective: Point a custom domain at App Service with the right DNS records and verification, and protect it with the right certificate and TLS settings.
engineer: DNS records you need: for a subdomain such as www, a CNAME to <app>.azurewebsites.net; for the root domain (apex) such as contoso.com, an A record to the app's inbound IP (or an alias record in Azure DNS); to prove you own it, a TXT record named asuid.<subdomain> (just asuid for the apex) holding the app's custom domain verification ID.
Tier needed: custom domains need Shared or higher. TLS certificates (bindings) need Basic or higher.

Certificate choices: App Service managed certificate, free and renews itself, but no wildcards and can't be exported; import from Key Vault, where the app needs access to the vault and renewals sync automatically; upload a PFX file, which must have a password, include the private key and use RSA 2048-bit or more; App Service Certificate, which you buy, stored in Key Vault.
Binding types: SNI SSL, the normal choice; IP-based SSL, which gives a dedicated IP.
TLS settings: turn on HTTPS Only to redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Set minimum TLS to 1.2. With Front Door or Application Gateway in front, you may need certificates there too.
Checking DNS: use nslookup or dig to check the CNAME, A and TXT records. Changes take time to spread, depending on the TTL.

example.title: Going live on www and the root domain
body: www.contoso.com gets a CNAME record, an asuid.www TXT record, and a free managed certificate. The root domain contoso.com gets an A record to the app's IP and an asuid TXT record. HTTPS Only sends all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
Later the team needs *.contoso.com. Managed certificates don't support wildcards, so they import a wildcard certificate from Key Vault.

architectureDecisions: Simple names use managed certificates: wildcards and certificates you want to rotate in one place go in Key Vault.
Always turn on HTTPS Only and TLS 1.2.

misconceptions.myth: A CNAME works on the root domain (contoso.com).
misconceptions.reality: No. DNS doesn't allow a CNAME at the root. Use an A record or an alias record.

misconceptions.myth: Free managed certificates can be exported.

comparisons.difference: Front Door can handle TLS and certificates at the edge, for apps behind it.
ACM gives free certificates for AWS endpoints.

troubleshooting.cause: The asuid TXT record is missing, wrong, or hasn't spread yet.
troubleshooting.fix: Check with nslookup -type=TXT asuid.www.contoso.com, and wait for the TTL.

troubleshooting.symptom: The browser shows a certificate warning.
troubleshooting.cause: No binding for that name, or the certificate doesn't match it.
troubleshooting.fix: Add an SNI binding with a matching certificate.

troubleshooting.symptom: You can't create a managed certificate for *.contoso.com.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Key Vault, or upload a wildcard PFX.

troubleshooting.cause: No private key, a weak key, or the wrong password.
troubleshooting.fix: Export the PFX with its private key and a password, RSA 2048-bit or more.

configuration.limits: Managed certificates: no wildcards, can't be exported
A PFX must include the private key
configuration.permissions: DNS Zone Contributor (Azure DNS) or access at your domain registrar
Key Vault Secrets User for the app's identity (for Key Vault certificates)
configuration.prerequisites: Basic tier or higher, for TLS
